Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio — The Pudding (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: Average back-to-back women rate across stations: 0.5%; Roughly 3 b2b women vs 245 b2b men in a single 24-hr listen

raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the public 'rule' against back-to-back women
raw_evidence.content: On 26 May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that women should be 'sprinkled' onto playlists like tomatoes in a salad — the lettuce being male artists like Luke Bryan, Blake Shelton and Keith Urban — and explicitly told programmers not to play two women back-to-back. The remarks ignited #SaladGate / #Tomato-gate, drawing public condemnation from Martina McBride, Miranda Lambert, Jennifer Nettles, and Leslie Fram. Hill said he had cut roughly half the women from his scheduling catalogue and observed a ratings bump — but he never tested the inverse for men. Country Aircheck publisher Lon Helton later defended the practice, saying program directors had been telling DJs not to play two women in a row 'since the 1960s.' The Pudding/SongData study is essentially a quantitative audit of whether that rule is still being followed eight years on.

raw_evidence.label: Headline finding: 0.5% of plays are women back-to-back
raw_evidence.content: Across all 29 stations and 19 dates, songs by women artists were played back-to-back an average of 0.5% of the time. Put another way: in a non-stop midnight-to-midnight listening session, you would expect to hear roughly 3 back-to-back songs by women — and 245 back-to-back songs by men. Out of 6,474 b2b pairs documented across the 19 days, only 64 (0.99%) were woman→woman pairs, while 4,231 (65.53%) were man→man pairs. Stations ranged from 0.03% (Cincinnati WUBE-FM) to 1.27% (Los Angeles KKGO-FM). For 17 of the 29 stations, the observed b2b rate for women fell below the 95% range produced by 1,000 random shuffles of that day's actual playlist, suggesting an active programming choice rather than chance.

raw_evidence.content: Across 182,848 song plays on 29 country radio stations in 2022, only 928 plays (0.51%) were a song by a women artist immediately following another song by a women artist. total_b2b_combined = SUMMARY['b2bCombinedGenderSongs_COUNT'].sum()

Source: SongData / Watson — Gender Representation on Country Format Radio (2019) (https://songdata.ca/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/SongData-Watson-Country-Airplay-S) Facts: Women peaked at 33.1% of Hot Country Songs in 1999; Women fell to 11.4% by 2015 Source: Tomato-gate — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomato-gate) Facts: Country Aircheck airplay share for women dropped from 13% (2016) to 10.4% (2017)

raw_evidence.label: Long decline of women on country charts
raw_evidence.content: Watson's earlier SongData reports show women's share of Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart peaked at 33.1% in 1999 and fell to 11.4% by 2015, averaging around 15% in the seven years that followed. The Country Aircheck airplay charts show a similar trajectory — women's share dropped from 13% in 2016 to 10.4% in 2017, the year following Tomato-gate. Many researchers tie this contraction to the 1996 Telecommunications Act, which removed national ownership caps and allowed iHeartMedia and Cumulus to consolidate hundreds of country stations onto centralized playlists.

Many researchers tie this contraction to the 1996 Telecommunications Act, which removed national ownership caps and allowed iHeartMedia and Cumulus to consolidate hundreds of country stations onto centralized playlists.

Source: the-pudding/country-radio-data analysis/ folder (https://github.com/the-pudding/country-radio-data) Facts: R scripts implement 1,000 shuffles per station per day; Reverse-roles script repeats the test treating men as the minority Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio — The Pudding (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: 17 of 29 stations fell below the 95% null-simulation range

raw_evidence.label: Statistical method: coin-flip simulation
raw_evidence.content: To test whether under-pairing of women is intentional, the analysts used the actual playlist for each station-day, kept the gender mix of songs constant, and re-shuffled the order 1,000 times. Each shuffle produced a hypothetical b2b-women count; together the 1,000 shuffles form a null distribution of 'how many b2b women you'd see by pure chance given that day's mix.' The observed b2b count is then compared to this distribution. If observed falls below the 2.5th percentile of the null distribution, that station-day is flagged as exhibiting active avoidance. Across the 29 stations, 17 (≈59%) showed the observed b2b-women count below their station's 95% null range, evidence the under-pairing is structural rather than random. The repo's R scripts (simulate_day_level.R, simulate_no_avoidance.R, reverse_roles.R) reproduce this calculation.

raw_evidence.label: Statistical significance — 25 of 29 stations under-pair women below chance
raw_evidence.content: Using the project's coin-flip simulation (1,000 random shuffles per station-day, holding gender mix constant), 25 of 29 stations have an observed b2b-women rate that falls below chance at p < 0.05; 18 stations have p = 0 (observed below ALL 1,000 simulations) — meaning under random scheduling the actual women-pairing count is essentially impossible. Only 4 stations (KAJA-SA, WUSN-Chicago, KASE-Austin, WTQR-Greensboro) fail to reach significance. This is empirical evidence the under-pairing is structural — programmed in — not random.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_06: Coin-flip significance test (p-values) ---
print("\n=== ana_06 ===")
# pval == 0 means observed b2b women count <= ALL 1000 simulated counts
# Pudding flagged anything below the 95% range
sig = PVALS.copy()
n_sig_women = (sig['pval_women'] < 0.05).sum()
print(f"Stations with p<0.05 for women under-pairing: {n_sig_women} / {len(sig)}")
print(f"Stations with p==0 (observed below ALL 1000 sims): {(sig['pval_women']==0).sum()}")
sig_sorted = sig.sort_values(['pval_women','stationName']).reset_index(drop=True)
print("All stations p-values:")
print(sig_sorted.to_string(index=False))
raw_evidence.output:
Stations with p<0.05 for women under-pairing: 25 / 29
Stations with p==0: 18
(See full p-value table)

sig_sorted = sig.sort_values(['pval_women','stationName']).reset_index(drop=True)
print("All stations p-values:")

# --- ana_05: Owner-level comparison ---

    only_women=('onlyWomenSongs_COUNT','sum'),
    b2b_men=('b2bMenSongs_COUNT','sum'),
).reset_index()

own = own.sort_values('b2b_women_pct')
print(own.to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: Owner-level concentration — small owners outperform iHeart & Cumulus
raw_evidence.content: Aggregating by station-owner: independent and small operators play women back-to-back more often than the major consolidators. Mount Wilson FM (single station, KKGO-LA) leads at 1.27% b2b-women, followed by Cox (1 station, 0.99%) and COX (1 station, 0.71%). The two largest country owners — iHeartMedia (8 stations) and Cumulus (5 stations) — sit near the bottom of the owner-weighted ranking at 0.40% each, despite controlling 13 of the 29 stations in the dataset. Hubbard (2 stations, 0.12%) and Steel City (2 stations, 0.27%) rank lowest of all.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_05: Owner-level comparison ---
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
own = SUMMARY.groupby('ownerName').agg(
    n_stations=('stationName','count'),
    total_songs=('total_COUNT','sum'),
    b2b_women=('b2bWomenSongs_COUNT','sum'),
    only_women=('onlyWomenSongs_COUNT','sum'),
    b2b_men=('b2bMenSongs_COUNT','sum'),
).reset_index()
own['women_airplay_pct'] = 100*own['only_women']/own['total_songs']
own['b2b_women_pct'] = 100*own['b2b_women']/own['total_songs']
own['b2b_men_pct'] = 100*own['b2b_men']/own['total_songs']
own = own.sort_values('b2b_women_pct')
print(own.to_string(index=False))
raw_evidence.output: Hubbard 0.12%, Steel City 0.27%, Cumulus 0.40%, iHeart 0.40%, Emmis 0.47%, Beasley 0.63%, Audacy 0.66%, COX 0.71%, Cox 0.99%, Mount Wilson 1.27%

raw_evidence.editorial_notes: iHeart 0.40%, Cumulus 0.40%, Hubbard 0.12% — name the owners, don't editorialize about them.

raw_evidence.label: Ownership concentration
raw_evidence.content: Of the 29 stations in the dataset, the dominant owners are iHeartMedia, Cumulus Media, Audacy, and Beasley Broadcast Group — a direct legacy of the 1996 Telecommunications Act, which lifted the ownership cap. Centralised programming decisions made by a small number of corporate consultants therefore propagate to dozens of local airwaves simultaneously. This is why a single consultant's 'rule of thumb' from 1960s programming manuals can still shape what listeners in 17 cities hear today.

sentences.summary: det_06: Daypart effect: women pushed to overnight. Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio — The Pudding (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: 46.1% of women's b2b plays during overnight (12am–6am); 19% during evenings (7pm–12am)

raw_evidence.label: Daypart effect: women pushed to overnight
raw_evidence.content: When women are played back-to-back, it overwhelmingly happens off-peak. 46.1% of women's b2b pairs air during the overnight block (12am–6am OVN), and another 19% during evenings (7pm–12am EVE) — together accounting for 65.1% of all women's b2bs. Prime drive-time hours (AM-Drive 6–10am and PM-Drive 3–7pm), when listenership and ad revenue peak, get only 25.1% combined. This concentrates the rare 'women heard together' moments in the hours when the smallest audience is listening.

19% during evenings (7pm–12am)

raw_evidence.label: Daypart exile: women's b2b clusters in overnight & evening
raw_evidence.content: Of the 928 back-to-back women plays, 42.6% (395) occur during the overnight block (12am–6am OVN) and 20.8% (193) during the evening (7pm–12am EVE) — 63.4% of all women's b2b moments happen when audiences are smallest. The two prime drive-time blocks together (AM-Drive 6–10am: 15.3%, PM-Drive 3–7pm: 9.3%) account for only 24.6%. The mid-day block contributes 12.1%. The 'tomato' is being served when the kitchen is empty.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_04: Daypart distribution of women's b2b plays ---
print("\n=== ana_04 ===")
# Sum across all stations
ovn = SUMMARY['b2bOVNwomenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
amd = SUMMARY['b2bAMDwomenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
mid = SUMMARY['b2bMIDwomenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
pmd = SUMMARY['b2bPMDwomenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
eve = SUMMARY['b2bEVEwomenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
total_dp = ovn + amd + mid + pmd + eve
print(f"b2b women OVN (12am-6am): {ovn} ({100*ovn/total_dp:.1f}%)")
print(f"b2b women AMD (6-10am):   {amd} ({100*amd/total_dp:.1f}%)")
print(f"b2b women MID (10-3pm):   {mid} ({100*mid/total_dp:.1f}%)")
print(f"b2b women PMD (3-7pm):    {pmd} ({100*pmd/total_dp:.1f}%)")
print(f"b2b women EVE (7pm-12am): {eve} ({100*eve/total_dp:.1f}%)")
print(f"OVN + EVE off-peak share: {100*(ovn+eve)/total_dp:.1f}%")
print(f"AMD + PMD drive-time share: {100*(amd+pmd)/total_dp:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Daypart exile
raw_evidence.editorial_notes: 42.6% OVN, 20.8% EVE, only 24.6% drive-time. The 'rare moments are at the smallest audiences' framing is critical.

sentences.summary: det_05: Race & intersectionality: women of color essentially invisible. Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio — The Pudding (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: Non-white b2b rate averages 0.38%; Of 11% women's airplay, 10.97% white women / 0.03% Black or biracial women

raw_evidence.label: Race & intersectionality: women of color essentially invisible
raw_evidence.content: Songs by non-white artists drew 0.38% of back-to-back plays on average. Of the 11% airplay share that went to women, 10.97% went to white women and only 0.03% went to Black or biracial women. Across the entire 19-day, 29-station dataset, only one back-to-back pair featuring an out LGBTQ+ artist was documented (Brothers Osborne / Hunter Hayes on Chicago's WUSN-FM, 7 February 2022), and the dataset contains zero plays of trans or non-binary artists. The combined 'gender minority' (women + mixed-gender ensembles) b2b rate is still only 1.5–2% on most stations — well below the share you'd expect from these artists' presence in the catalogue.

sentences.summary: det_07: Catalogue concentration: 3 women carry current rotation. Source: They Won't Play a Lady-O on Country Radio — The Pudding (https://pudding.cool/2023/05/country-radio/) Facts: Top 3 current women (Barrett, Ballerini, Wilson) = 52.5% of current-women airplay; Top 3 current men (Jelly Roll, Allen, Zac Brown Band) = 20.4% of current-men airplay

raw_evidence.label: Catalogue concentration: 3 women carry current rotation
raw_evidence.content: Among 'current' (newly released) songs played, the top 3 women — Gabby Barrett, Kelsea Ballerini, and Lainey Wilson — accounted for 52.5% of all current-women plays. raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the public 'rule' against back-to-back women
raw_evidence.content: On 26 May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that women should be 'sprinkled' onto playlists like tomatoes in a salad — the lettuce being male artists like Luke Bryan, Blake Shelton and Keith Urban — and explicitly told programmers not to play two women back-to-back. The remarks ignited #SaladGate / #Tomato-gate, drawing public condemnation from Martina McBride, Miranda Lambert, Jennifer Nettles, and Leslie Fram. Hill said he had cut roughly half the women from his scheduling catalogue and observed a ratings bump — but he never tested the inverse for men. Country Aircheck publisher Lon Helton later defended the practice, saying program directors had been telling DJs not to play two women in a row 'since the 1960s.' The Pudding/SongData study is essentially a quantitative audit of whether that rule is still being followed eight years on.

raw_evidence.label: 0.5% — back-to-back women vs 65% back-to-back men
raw_evidence.content: Across 182,848 song plays on 29 country radio stations in 2022, only 928 plays (0.51%) were a song by a women artist immediately following another song by a women artist. Plays where a man's song followed another man's song accounted for 118,861 plays — 65.01% of all airtime. The mean station-level rate was 0.50% women back-to-back vs 65.05% men back-to-back. Among all back-to-back pairs in the dataset (women+men+mixed combined = 120,646), women-on-women pairs are 0.77% and men-on-men pairs are 98.52%. The men-to-women back-to-back ratio is 128:1.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_01: Headline - back-to-back women vs men gap ---
print("\n=== ana_01 ===")
total_songs = SUMMARY['total_COUNT'].sum()
total_b2b_women = SUMMARY['b2bWomenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
total_b2b_men   = SUMMARY['b2bMenSongs_COUNT'].sum()
total_b2b_mixed = SUMMARY['b2bMixedGenderSongs_COUNT'].sum()
total_b2b_combined = SUMMARY['b2bCombinedGenderSongs_COUNT'].sum()
# total b2b pairs = sum across all categories (per station)
# instead, use b2b_men + b2b_women + b2b_mixed as approximation of all b2b pairs
# More accurately: sum of any consecutive same-category, but for headline use these three
total_b2b_any = total_b2b_women + total_b2b_men + total_b2b_mixed
print(f"Total songs: {total_songs:,}")
print(f"b2b women count: {total_b2b_women:,}")
print(f"b2b men count: {total_b2b_men:,}")
print(f"b2b mixed-gender count: {total_b2b_mixed:,}")
print(f"b2b women % of all songs: {100*total_b2b_women/total_songs:.2f}%")
print(f"b2b men % of all songs: {100*total_b2b_men/total_songs:.2f}%")
print(f"b2b women % of b2b pairs (women+men+mixed): {100*total_b2b_women/total_b2b_any:.2f}%")
print(f"b2b men % of b2b pairs (women+men+mixed): {100*total_b2b_men/total_b2b_any:.2f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Tomato-gate: the public 'rule' against back-to-back women
raw_evidence.content: On 26 May 2015, country-radio consultant Keith Hill told the trade publication Country Aircheck that women should be 'sprinkled' onto playlists like tomatoes in a salad — the lettuce being male artists like Luke Bryan, Blake Shelton and Keith Urban — and explicitly told programmers not to play two women back-to-back. The remarks ignited #SaladGate / #Tomato-gate, drawing public condemnation from Martina McBride, Miranda Lambert, Jennifer Nettles, and Leslie Fram. Hill said he had cut roughly half the women from his scheduling catalogue and observed a ratings bump — but he never tested the inverse for men. Country Aircheck publisher Lon Helton later defended the practice, saying program directors had been telling DJs not to play two women in a row 'since the 1960s.' The Pudding/SongData study is essentially a quantitative audit of whether that rule is still being followed eight years on.
